newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss central bank charts difficult policy course.
newsitem.headline: Swiss central bank charts difficult policy course.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) will continue to plot a pragmatic policy course for as long as possible, but Chairman Hans Meyer is the first to admit that the path it is following is not an easy one.
The SNB has conducted a generous monetary policy for more than two years.

Meyer said the bank will not shift to a stricter policy until the Swiss economy is firmly on the path to recovery, and said it will continue to take exchange rate fluctuations into account. But it also remains vigilant on inflation.
"We are convinced that this policy is adequate... but we don't have any illusions that we are in a difficult situation," he said at the SNB's summer news conference.
Meyer has just finished his first year at the helm of the SNB, where he has worked for his entire professional career.
The SNB has stressed repeatedly that its main worry, besides the weak economy, is what happens to the Swiss franc before planned introduction of the single European currency in 1999.

Worries that the new currency could be weak have drawn investors into the Swiss franc in recent months. But some economists even see danger of a reverse situation, in which the Swiss franc drops suddenly and money floods into the system.
Although SNB policy has mostly aimed of late at keeping the franc from appreciating to a point where it damages exports, it also sees its foremost duty as ensuring stable prices.

Meyer noted that the SNB is even seeking some constitutional changes designed to ensure its independence, while explicitly stating that its main role is keeping prices stable. He said this was the best way the SNB could serve the Swiss economy.
The SNB has also been seeing some signs that the economy, flat for most of this decade, is starting to turn around.
The key to fighting inflation will be in the timing, said Meyer, or acting at "the right moment on the curve".

The SNB has said in the past that any policy changes affect domestic prices after a lag of about two to three years. However, the current scenario does not appear threatening in terms of inflation, given the slow pace of the recovery.
Meyer also said that strong rises in the SNB's monetary base -- the key yardstick used for setting long-term policy -- were not worrying even though the aggregate is above target.

The M0 base, consisting of sight deposits and notes in circulation, would be growing at the projected pace of one percent per annum if special factors were excluded such as a big rise in large-denomination notes and a shift of deposits into SNB accounts from postal giro accounts last year.
He said the SNB was still trying to determine why the amount of big notes has jumped in recent months. "One should not speculate too much before the current investigations are completed," he said.

Bruno Gehrig, one of the SNB's three board members, told reporters following the media briefing that the SNB has also been paying more attention to short-term interest rates set on its routine money market operations.
Such operations include purchases of government paper at a set rate, which adds liquidity to the system.

Gehrig said the SNB has oriented itself more strongly to money market rates since last August and September, when it began to add liquidity to the money market aggressively to counteract a rise in the Swiss franc.
He said that this focus, as opposed to looking at money aggregates, was directed at the SNB's day-to-day operations.
However, he said that this did not mean that the SNB will deviate from its long-term policy of focusing on aggregates.
-- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
